scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7082: HELP!! My laptop and the one RIGHT NEXT to it can't see
each other any more!! We swap files constantly and now -- nothing, in either
direction, since this morning. Something around the office switch must be
wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look at whatever connects our two
desks so our laptops talk again -- we share everything for the Friday
handover!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. Laptop2 and Laptop3 are both on VLAN 10
  (172.16.10.0/24), attached through switch1, in the same broadcast domain --
  this is a pure intra-subnet, Layer-2 path that does not even involve router0.
  Laptop2 reaches Laptop3 with 0% loss; switch1 forwards VLAN 10 frames normally
  and no port is blocking or err-disabled. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of an L2/switch fault that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Laptop2 cannot reach its
same-VLAN neighbor Laptop3 -- is NOT reproducible: both hosts sit on VLAN 10
(172.16.10.0/24) behind switch1, and Laptop2 reaches Laptop3 directly (same
subnet, no routing) with 0% loss. switch1 forwards VLAN 10 frames normally and
there is no blocked, err-disabled, or shut port on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the intra-VLAN L2 path is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the
Laptop2->Laptop3 path, finds it working, confirms both interfaces are up on the
same subnet, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a switch1 drop, a
blocking/err-disabled port, or a VLAN mismatch to satisfy the ticket is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** iptables FORWARD chain on router6 — three DROP rules targeting all traffic ingressing on eth2 (the WAN uplink to router3).

**Mechanism:** Router6 serves as the inter-VLAN gateway and WAN edge for the mswitch2 segment. Its eth0 faces VLAN50 (172.18.50.0/24, including laptop4 and laptop5), eth1 faces VLAN51 (172.18.51.0/24, including pc15–pc18), and eth2 is the uplink to router3 (10.50.1.0/24). The FORWARD chain contains three DROP rules all matching `--in-interface eth2`: one for TCP (proto 6), one for UDP (proto 17), and one catch-all that matches all remaining protocols including ICMP. A single narrow ACCEPT precedes them for TCP port 80 from 172.16.10.0/24 to 172.18.51.1 only. Every reply packet returning from the wider network (routing table shows RIP-learned routes via eth2 for all external subnets) is discarded at router6 before it can be forwarded to either local VLAN. Outbound packets leave normally; inbound replies are silently dropped. At the time of inspection, 18 ICMP packets (1 512 bytes) had already been killed by the all-protocols DROP rule, directly corroborating the observed ping timeouts.

**Localization:** router6, iptables FORWARD chain, all three DROP rules with `--in-interface eth2`.

**Root cause:** Overly restrictive iptables rules on router6 block all return traffic from the WAN side, completely isolating VLAN50 and VLAN51 hosts from the rest of the network.

**Fix:** Delete the three DROP rules from router6's FORWARD chain with `iptables -D FORWARD` matching each rule, and remove them from the startup script (e.g., `/etc/network/interfaces` or `/etc/startup`) so they do not reapply on reboot.

per_axis.rationale: The agent's writeup centers on router6/iptables and does not state that Laptop2 and Laptop3 are both on VLAN10 behind switch1 and verify they reach each other with 0% loss.

Investigation log records direct tests (pings, ip addr), device link/state checks, and an iptables inspection whose findings are summarized in the agent notes; the conclusions follow logically from those observations and the checks performed cover the plausible alternatives. A couple of iptables snippets were truncated but the agent notes supply the observed DROP rules and counters used in the causal chain.
